x.ASV: Oh come, let us sing unto Jehovah; Let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation.
x.Darby: Come, let us sing aloud to Jehovah, let us shout for joy to the rock of our salvation;
x.KJV: O come, let us sing unto the Lord: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation.
x.YLT: Come, we sing to Jehovah, We shout to the rock of our salvation.

nt: Here the writer is speaking as if Yahweh were a **rock**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how “rock” and “of my salvation” are translated in [Psalms 18:46](../018/046.md). Alternate translation: [to our protector and savior]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to our steadfast savior]

x.ASV: Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving; Let us make a joyful noise unto him with psalms.
x.Darby: Let us come before his face with thanksgiving; let us shout aloud unto him with psalms.
x.KJV: Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving, and make a joyful noise unto him with psalms.
x.YLT: We come before His face with thanksgiving, With psalms we shout to Him.

nt: Here, **his face** represents being in the presence of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Let us go into his presence]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thanksgiving**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as we thank him]

x.ASV: For Jehovah is a great God, And a great King above all gods.
x.Darby: For Jehovah is a greatGod, and a great king above allgods.
x.KJV: For the Lord is a great God, and a great King above all gods.
x.YLT: For a great God is Jehovah, And a great king over all gods.

nt: The term “god,” when applied to a being other than Yahweh, can refer to an idol, but, as here, it can also refer to any lesser spirit being. Alternate translation: [above any other spiritual being]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh were actually positioned **above all gods** in a physical sense. He means that Yahweh is superior to all other gods. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who is superior to all other gods]

x.ASV: In his hand are the deep places of the earth; The heights of the mountains are his also.
x.Darby: In his hand are the deep places of the earth; the heights of the mountains are his also:
x.KJV: In his hand are the deep places of the earth: the strength of the hills is his also.
x.YLT: In whose hand are the deep places of earth, And the strong places of hills are His.

nt: The psalmist is using **in his hand** as a common expression of his culture to mean “in his control” or “under his authority.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in his control]

The psalmist is referring to all of the earth by naming two extremes, **the depths of the earth** and **the heights of the mountains**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [every part of the earth; they all]

The psalmist is using **are to him** as a common expression of his culture to mean “belong to him” or “are his.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are his]

x.ASV: The sea is his, and he made it; And his hands formed the dry land.
x.Darby: The sea is his, and he made it, and his hands formed the dry [land].
x.KJV: The sea is his, and he made it: and his hands formed the dry land.
x.YLT: Whose is the sea, and He made it, And His hands formed the dry land.

nt: The psalmist is using **who to him is** as a common expression of his culture to mean “who owns.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who owns]

The writer is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he made it** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh is the one who made the sea. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and it was he who made it]

Here the word **hands** represents the action of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he himself formed the dry land]

x.ASV: Oh come, let us worship and bow down; Let us kneel before Jehovah our Maker:
x.Darby: Come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before Jehovah our Maker.
x.KJV: O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the Lord our maker.
x.YLT: Come in, we bow ourselves, and we bend, We kneel before Jehovah our Maker.

nt: The phrases **bow down** and **kneel** describe symbolic actions by which people showed submission and reverence to God. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of these actions in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and show that we submit]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of]

x.ASV: For he is our God, And we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. To-day, oh that ye would hear his voice!
x.Darby: For he is ourGod; and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand. To-day if ye hear his voice,
x.KJV: For he is our God; and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. To day if ye will hear his voice,
x.YLT: For He is our God, and we the people of His pasture, And the flock of His hand, To-day, if to His voice ye hearken,

nt: The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the God whom we worship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the God whom we worship]

The psalmist is speaking as if the people were like God’s sheep in **his pasture**. He means that the people are like God’s sheep that he provides for. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people who belong to him]

The psalmist is speaking here of God’s people as if they were **the flock of his hand**. This image portrays God as a shepherd who personally cares for and guides his people like sheep. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the group that he directs and guards]

The psalmist says **if only you would listen** to introduce a wish that God’s people would obey him. Use a natural method in your language for introducing a wish. Alternate translation: [I wish you would listen]
Here, **voice** represents what God says. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to what he says]

x.ASV: Harden not your heart, as at Meribah, As in the day of Massah in the wilderness;
x.Darby: Harden not your heart, as at Meribah, as [in] the day of Massah, in the wilderness;
x.KJV: Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, and as in the day of temptation in the wilderness:
x.YLT: Harden not your heart as in Meribah, As in the day of Massah in the wilderness,

nt: The psalmist is using **harden your heart** as a common expression of his culture to mean “become stubborn” or “refuse to listen and obey.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not be obstinate]
The words **Meribah** and **Massah** are the names of places.

x.ASV: When your fathers tempted me, Proved me, and saw my work.
x.Darby: When your fathers tempted me, proved me, and saw my work.
x.KJV: When your fathers tempted me, proved me, and saw my work.
x.YLT: Where your fathers have tried Me, Have proved Me, yea, have seen My work.

nt: The terms **tested me** and **tried me** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [tested my patience] or [refused to trust me]

x.ASV: Forty years long was I grieved with that generation, And said, It is a people that do err in their heart, And they have not known my ways:
x.Darby: Forty years was I grieved with the generation, and said, It is a people that do err in their heart, and they have not known my ways;
x.KJV: Forty years long was I grieved with this generation, and said, It is a people that do err in their heart, and they have not known my ways:
x.YLT: Forty years I am weary of the generation, And I say, `A people erring in heart--they! And they have not known My ways:'

nt: Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [For forty years]

God is using **wandering of heart** as a common expression of his culture to mean “tending to stray” or “lacking in commitment.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [blowing hot and cold] or [lacking in commitment]

The pronouns **they, they** refer to the people of Israel whom God is describing. The psalmist is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they have not known** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that these very people failed to know God’s ways. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the emphasis here. Alternate translation: [and those very people have not known]

Here God is speaking of how he wants people to live as if that were **ways** that people could walk along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the way that I teach people to live]

x.ASV: Wherefore I sware in my wrath, That they should not enter into my rest.
x.Darby: So that I swore in mine anger, that they should not enter into my rest.
x.KJV: Unto whom I sware in my wrath that they should not enter into my rest.
x.YLT: Where I sware in Mine anger, `If they come in unto My rest--!'

nt: God is using **in my nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in my anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in my anger]

Following the custom of the culture, God is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (**If they enter into my rest**) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [If they enter into my rest, then I am not Yahweh]
